document.title: Pakistan: Reaction to Afghanistan Strikes
document.authors: U.S. Department of State (Assistant Secretary for South Asian Affairs Karl F. Inderfurth to the Secretary of State)
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan's Bin Laden Policy
document.note: [Confidential] Information memorandum written the day after U.S. missile strikes in Afghanistan and Sudan. Clinton calls Nawaz Sharif; the conversation is cordial, but Islamabad decides to take a hard line against the strikes. Inderfurth does not expect the negative reaction to subside. The Sharif government operates amid conspiracy theories and cannot condemn bin Laden without alienating religious parties. Excised.

events.description: President Clinton telephoned Nawaz Sharif; offered to work with Pakistan to establish facts on the reported missile in Pakistan; Sharif agreed to constructive approach in London talks.
US strikes against terrorist targets in Afghanistan (Bin Laden strikes); reports a cruise missile hit inside Pakistan, later retracted.
Sartaj Aziz made a statement in the Senate denying Pakistani assistance or advance notification.
Demonstrations against the strikes in Islamabad, Karachi, Peshawar.
Planned London meeting between Strobe Talbott and Shamshad Ahmad on nonproliferation.
Clinton telephoned Nawaz Sharif regarding the strikes; Sharif agreed Pakistan would attend London talks with a constructive approach.
US strikes against terrorist (Bin Laden) targets in Afghanistan; reports a cruise missile fell inside Pakistan, later retracted by Pakistan.
Foreign Minister Sartaj Aziz made a Senate statement denouncing the strikes and denying Pakistani assistance or notification; ambassadors were called in and a protest delivered to the US DCM.
Demonstrations against the strikes held in Islamabad, Karachi and Peshawar; right-wing Islamic parties condemned the strikes.
Planned London talks on nonproliferation between Deputy Secretary Talbott and Foreign Secretary Shamshad Ahmad the week after the memo.

key_claims: Pakistan's government denied assisting or being notified of the US strikes and retracted claims a cruise missile fell inside Pakistan.
Public reaction was negative, with demonstrations in Islamabad, Karachi and Peshawar and Islamic parties condemning the strikes.
Inderfurth worried about the vulnerability of the 70 US officials remaining in Pakistan.
Embassy Islamabad judged Pakistan's most sincere reaction was exasperation at domestic difficulties in keeping religious parties off the street.
Sharif agreed to a constructive approach in the London nonproliferation talks, though cooperation on CTBT could become harder.
